content: Economists use the term representative agent to describe a typical individual of a certain type, such as a typical consumer or a typical firm. In technical terms, an economic model is said to have a representative agent if all agents of the same type are identical. Alternatively, a model may also be described as having a representative agent when agents differ but behave in such a way that the aggregate of their choices is mathematically equivalent to the decision of a single individual or a group of identical individuals. Models that include many different agents whose choices cannot be aggregated in this manner are referred to as heterogeneous agent models. The concept of the representative agent can be traced back to the late 19th century. Francis Edgeworth introduced the term representative particular in 1881, while Alfred Marshall introduced the idea of a representative firm in his 1890 work, Principles of Economics. However, the notion gained greater prominence and controversy after Robert Lucas, Jr.'s critique of econometric policy evaluation in the 1970s, which spurred the development of microfoundations for macroeconomics. Today, many macroeconomic models explicitly incorporate optimization problems for representative agents, which may represent either consumers, producers, or both. The individual demand or supply curves derived from these models are then used as aggregate demand or supply curves. When economists analyze the behavior of a representative agent, it is often because it is simpler to focus on one typical decision-maker rather than simultaneously analyzing the decisions of many different individuals. However, the representative agent assumption must be abandoned when individual differences are central to the question being studied. For example, while a representative consumer might suffice for general consumption analysis, studying health insurance would likely require a heterogeneous agent model, as health insurance inherently involves transferring money from relatively healthy individuals to those with costly illnesses. James Hartley (1997) discusses the reasons for the prominence of representative agent modeling in contemporary macroeconomics. Robert Lucas's critique in 1976 highlighted that policy recommendations based on observed past macroeconomic relationships might fail to account for behavioral changes by economic agents, which could alter the macroeconomic relationships themselves. Lucas argued that this issue could be avoided by using models that explicitly describe the decision-making processes of individual agents. In such models, economists could analyze policy changes by recalculating the decision problems of each agent under the new policy and then aggregating these decisions to determine the macroeconomic effects. Lucas's argument convinced many macroeconomists to adopt microfounded models, though these were technically more challenging to construct. As a result, early general equilibrium macroeconomic models often simplified by assuming representative agents. Models with many heterogeneous agents are far more complex and remain a relatively new area of economic research. Critics of the representative agent approach, such as Alan Kirman (1992), argue that it ignores valid aggregation concerns and can lead to the fallacy of composition. Kirman provides an example where the representative agent's preferences conflict with those of all individuals in the economy, rendering policy recommendations based on the representative agent's welfare illegitimate. He concludes that reducing a group of heterogeneous agents to a single representative agent is not merely an analytical convenience but is both unjustified and leads to conclusions that are usually misleading and often wrong. Kirman suggests that the representative agent approach deserves a decent burial as a fundamentally flawed method of economic analysis. Alternative approaches to the representative agent model include agent-based simulation models, which can handle many heterogeneous agents, and dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models with heterogeneous agents. While the latter is technically challenging, it is becoming more common in economic research, as noted by José-Víctor Ríos-Rull (1995).
